title: FuriosaAI Raises $620 Mn Series D At $2.9 Bn Valuation To Scale AI Inference Chips
summary: FuriosaAI raises $620 million Series D at $2.9 billion valuation for AI inference chips
detailed: South Korean AI chip designer FuriosaAI has raised KRW 820 billion (approximately $620 million) in a Series D round, reaching a post-money valuation of $2.9 billion.
The company builds inference accelerators for data centers, focusing on its RNGD chip and full-stack software integration.
RNGD entered mass production in January 2026, with production targets set at 20,000 units in 2026 and over 40,000 units in 2027, backed by customers like LG Group, Samsung SDS, and Upstage.
sentences: FuriosaAI, a South Korean AI chip designer, has raised KRW 820 billion, or about $620 million, in a Series D round.
The round takes its post-money valuation to roughly $2.9 billion.
The company builds inference accelerators for data centres.
It will use the money to expand production of its RNGD chip, strengthen its software ecosystem and speed up development of a third-generation accelerator.
FuriosaAI was founded in 2017.
It designs AI accelerators for inference, which is the stage where a trained model answers a query or generates an output.

That full-stack approach matters in inference.
A chip is only useful if the software above it can run the models customers already use, and most challengers lose deals on that point rather than on raw speed.
June Paik, co-founder and chief executive, makes the case simply: a model is trained once, but it runs billions of times in production.
Inference is the recurring cost, and every percentage point of efficiency shows up in an operator’s monthly bill.
RNGD targets models running at up to about 100 tokens per second per user, which the company says is the range that matters for enterprise workloads.
It is optimised for open models rather than for a single vendor’s flagship.
Production volume is the part investors watch closest.
A chip startup can win design wins for years without shipping at scale, and the market eventually stops paying for design wins alone.
RNGD entered mass production in January 2026.
FuriosaAI expects to produce 20,000 accelerators in 2026 and more than 40,000 in 2027.
LG Group runs its EXAONE deployments on RNGD.
Samsung SDS launched a commercial NPU-as-a-service on the chip in July.
Upstage uses it to serve live search summarisation for millions of users.
A listed conglomerate, its IT services arm and a well-known AI startup are the kind of references that shorten a sales cycle.
For FuriosaAI, they also answer the first question every buyer asks about a new chip.
Data centre operators are now limited by power and cooling more than by floor space.
A chip that delivers more inference within the same power envelope is worth more than a faster chip that needs a new facility.
FuriosaAI positions RNGD exactly there.
It pairs high-bandwidth memory with a power-efficient design, and it markets the chip as sustainable compute rather than as the fastest option.
That framing travels well in Korea and Europe, where energy costs and carbon reporting are board-level issues.
Three things will decide whether FuriosaAI becomes a durable competitor to Nvidia and the hyperscaler chips.
The first is production yield.
Doubling output to 40,000 units in 2027 only helps if the wafers come back usable.
The second is the Broadcom partnership for third-generation chips.
Working with a major ASIC partner signals that the company expects to scale beyond its own design capacity.
The third is software lock-in.
If customers can move a model onto RNGD in days rather than months, the chip becomes a genuine alternative.
If it takes months, FuriosaAI stays a niche supplier with a good product.
